{{Short description|Type of measure in measure theory}}
{{refimprove|date=January 2026}}
In [[mathematics]], strict positivity is a concept in [[measure theory]]. Intuitively, a '''strictly positive measure''' is one that is "nowhere zero", or that is zero "only on points".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Van Casteren |first1=Jan A. |title=Strictly Positive Radon Measures |journal=Journal of the London Mathematical Society |date=February 1994 |volume=49 |issue=1 |pages=109–123 |doi=10.1112/jlms/49.1.109}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Bogachev |first1=Vladimir I. |title=Measure theory |date=2007 |publisher=Springer |location=Berlin ; New York |isbn=978-3-540-34513-8 |edition=1}}</ref>

==Definition==

Let <math>(X, T)</math> be a [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] [[topological space]] and let <math>\Sigma</math> be a [[Sigma algebra|<math>\sigma</math>-algebra]] on <math>X</math> that contains the topology <math>T</math> (so that every [[open set]] is a [[measurable set]], and <math>\Sigma</math> is at least as fine as the [[Borel sigma algebra|Borel <math>\sigma</math>-algebra]] on <math>X</math>). Then a measure <math>\mu</math> on <math>(X, \Sigma)</math> is called '''strictly positive''' if every non-empty open subset of <math>X</math> has strictly positive measure.

More concisely, <math>\mu</math> is strictly positive [[if and only if]] for all <math>U \in T</math> such that <math>U \neq \varnothing, \mu (U) > 0.</math>

==Examples==

* [[Counting measure]] on any set <math>X</math> (with any topology) is strictly positive.
* [[Dirac measure]] is usually not strictly positive unless the topology <math>T</math> is particularly "coarse" (contains "few" sets). For example, <math>\delta_0</math> on the [[real line]] <math>\R</math> with its usual Borel topology and <math>\sigma</math>-algebra is not strictly positive; however, if <math>\R</math> is equipped with the trivial topology <math>T = \{\varnothing, \R\},</math> then <math>\delta_0</math> is strictly positive. This example illustrates the importance of the topology in determining strict positivity.
* [[Gaussian measure]] on [[Euclidean space]] <math>\R^n</math> (with its Borel topology and <math>\sigma</math>-algebra) is strictly positive.
** [[Wiener measure]] on the space of continuous paths in <math>\R^n</math> is a strictly positive measure &mdash; Wiener measure is an example of a Gaussian measure on an infinite-dimensional space.
* [[Lebesgue measure]] on <math>\R^n</math> (with its Borel topology and <math>\sigma</math>-algebra) is strictly positive.
* The [[trivial measure]] is never strictly positive, regardless of the space <math>X</math> or the topology used, except when <math>X</math> is empty.

==Properties==

* If <math>\mu</math> and <math>\nu</math> are two measures on a measurable topological space <math>(X, \Sigma),</math> with <math>\mu</math> strictly positive and also [[absolutely continuous]] with respect to <math>\nu,</math> then <math>\nu</math> is strictly positive as well. The proof is simple: let <math>U \subseteq X</math> be an arbitrary open set; since <math>\mu</math> is strictly positive, <math>\mu(U) > 0;</math> by absolute continuity, <math>\nu(U) > 0</math> as well.
* Hence, strict positivity is an [[Invariant (mathematics)|invariant]] with respect to [[equivalence of measures]].
* Any [[uniformly distributed measure]] on a [[metric space]] is strictly positive. Because if there is an nonempty open set with zero measure, then the measure of some open balls will be zero, which contradicts the definition of uniformly distributed'''.'''

==See also==

* {{annotated link|Support (measure theory)}} − a measure is strictly positive [[if and only if]] its support is the whole space.
